Historically, however—that is, in the specifically human sphere—human beings do know how technically to “make” citizens on the basis of definite theoretical conceptions of humanity.
Through its political work of education, the state “makes” its citizens in much the same technical sense that technology makes airplanes.
But this kind of “production” has the same limitations as the production of machines.
Technology knows how to make machines, but it cannot itself produce everything from which those machines are made.
The same is true of the state.
It may possess the art of “making” citizens, but its activity does not encompass every purely human element that exists in them.
The aluminum in an airplane, for example, remains what it is independently of the fuselage or the technical form imposed on it.
Something similar is true of the citizen. Many aspects of a citizen’s human life remain untouched by the political shape or finish imposed by the state.
Those unshaped aspects obviously cannot serve to “verify” the corresponding elements in our knowledge of human beings.
The existence of any state therefore guarantees the presence of some true but partial knowledge of humanity.
That knowledge can consequently be regarded as a part of perfect or universal knowledge.
In this sense, politics justifies the existence of philosophy in its anthropological dimension, just as technology guarantees it in its cosmological dimension.
But the philosophical ideal—omniscience—can be reached only through the exhaustive development of both technology and politics.
Technology must teach us how to make everything that exists in nature.
Politics must become capable of shaping everything that constitutes the specifically human existence of human beings.
Philosophy therefore rejects anything that places either internal or external limits on the state’s work of public education.
It must oppose every nation-state that consciously restricts its activity to particular national or racial sections of humanity.
It must reject the idea that education should come to an end at a particular age.
It must oppose every form of political “liberalism” which declares whole areas of human life to lie outside state control.
Philosophy can be completely satisfied only under a universal state that, through its work of education, assimilates the whole life of all human beings.
In other words, as we already know, philosophy can attain omniscience only in a worldwide communist society.
But because states already exist, philosophy already has the right to regard itself genuinely as philosophy: as a path leading toward omniscience.
And here again, just as with our knowledge of nature, philosophy studies concrete reality.
It does not merely know what human beings know about themselves. It also understands how and why they know it.
Philosophy must therefore also be a theory of the true knowledge human beings have of themselves.
And as such, it must be a theory of social and political life—that is, a theory of struggle.
In all these respects, political verification of anthropological knowledge parallels technical verification of cosmological knowledge.
But there is one essential difference between the two. In one respect, this difference makes philosophy’s task easier. In another, it makes it considerably harder.
When we transform a theory into objective reality through technical work, reality itself can establish whether that theory is true or false.
Yet natural reality directly judges only the real things produced on the basis of technical theories, not the theories themselves.
The author of the theory still has to interpret nature’s evidence for or against it. Nature does not tell him which precise part of his theory proved true or false.
In one sense, a state behaves in exactly the same way.
By continuing to exist or by collapsing, the state “judges” the political realizations of human theories, rather than directly judging the theories themselves.
But in another sense, because the state is not a natural reality but a human reality, it can also testify directly about the theories themselves and identify exactly what is true or false in them.
Political verification therefore has an undeniable advantage over technical verification.
And this advantage is especially valuable for a philosophical theory of human knowledge.

In the perfect communist society, true knowledge will be guaranteed not only “silently” by the very existence of a society founded on that knowledge, but also explicitly and publicly by the testimony of the competent institutions.

Yet although the difference between politics and technology makes the idea of true knowledge about humanity—and especially of true philosophy—easier in this respect, in another respect it makes the problem much more difficult.
The natural world is, so to speak, independent of time. It remains eternally unchanged.
An airplane that flies today would also fly ten thousand years from now. If it had been possible to build the same airplane ten thousand years ago, it would have flown then just as it does now.
The human world is fundamentally different.
It is historical through and through.
The human beings who enter it today are not the same as those who entered it a thousand years ago, and they will not be the same as those who enter it a thousand years from now.
The principles that once allowed the Assyrian state to exist therefore cannot serve today as stable foundations for every form of state.
Nor can the foundations of contemporary British politics necessarily serve the political life of future humanity.
This throws the whole idea of politically verifying a theory into question—including, in particular, the testimony given by states about the theories presented to them.
Something condemned as a dangerous lie by Assyrian censorship might today be recognized as true by British organs of propaganda, only to be condemned once again as false by the state of the future.
We will return at the end of this chapter to the related problems raised by this difficult question.
For now, however, one point must already be stressed.

If we accept the existence of history as an undeniable fact—that is, if we accept that human beings change fundamentally over time—we can avoid the complete scepticism that denies the possibility of knowledge about humanity only by appealing to the Hegelian-Marxist conception of world history as a kind of international tribunal.
We must assume that humanity “judges” during the course of its historical development in the same way that a state judges its citizens and the theories they put forward.
Only the theory recognized by humanity “at the end of time” can be regarded as definitively, absolutely true.
In other words, the true theory will be the one adopted by the final—absolute or ideal—state: the single state that will exist eternally and without further change.
Once again, then, we arrive at the conclusion that absolute knowledge of humanity can only be omniscience, verified by the integral state—that is, by communist society.
For the moment, however, our subject is not omniscience but philosophy: the path that leads toward it, or the true but partial knowledge that can be regarded as an embryo of universal truth.
Here we need to repeat the point once more: political verification makes the possibility of philosophical knowledge entirely secure.

First, there are theories about human beings that must be presupposed if we are to explain the possibility of any political life under any state at all. These theories can already be regarded as definitively true.
Second, we can identify theories that have been presupposed, either tacitly or explicitly, by every known state. These too can be regarded as true with a high degree of confidence.
And finally, even now we can sometimes decide between different theories that different states, at different times, have regarded as true or false.

At present, for example, the fact that England is not the property of the Assyrian state, whereas Mesopotamia is British property, means that, whatever other disagreements may remain, the knowledge contained in contemporary English political theory contains more truth than the knowledge embodied—tacitly or explicitly—in the political theory recognized by the Assyrian state.
Taking everything we have said together, then, we can maintain that technical and political verification establish, in principle, the possibility of attaining perfect knowledge.
And this also establishes the possibility of philosophy: of true knowledge that knows itself to be partial and imperfect, but understands itself as a constituent part of future omniscience.

We must stress once again, however, that if philosophy differs from wisdom only because its knowledge is partial, it is philosophy—that is, an aspiration toward wisdom and a path leading to it—only when it is fully aware of the partial character of its knowledge.
It must know how and why its knowledge is partial.
And it must explain how and why that knowledge can continue to expand without any fixed limit.

Philosophy must therefore know that it can enlarge its knowledge only by using the results supplied by the political and technical verification of human knowledge of the world—that is, knowledge of nature and history.
It must also understand that the very character of this verification makes its knowledge necessarily partial and therefore imperfect.
As long as technology has not become universal, philosophical knowledge is necessarily limited in space. Its knowledge of nature—its Cosmology—remains incomplete.

And as long as historical development continues, as long as the universal state has not been established, philosophical knowledge is necessarily limited in time. Its knowledge of the historical world—its Anthropology—remains incomplete.
As long as this remains the case, philosophy must “call into question” everything presented to it as “absolute truth,” including whatever philosophy itself may be tempted to regard in this way.
For philosophy knows that something declared true by the political tribunal of one particular historical moment may be declared false by the final judgment of the tribunal of world history.
Partial knowledge becomes philosophical knowledge, in other words, only when it contains, so to speak, the idea of omniscience within itself.
At that point it appears not only as philosophical knowledge but also as a philosophical problem.
Once philosophy becomes conscious of itself as partial knowledge striving toward universality, it necessarily understands itself as an attempt to turn every form of positive knowledge into a problem.
This brings us to the second aspect of philosophy.

Because philosophy exists as partial or fragmentary knowledge, it necessarily appears not simply—and ultimately not even mainly—as the art of giving the best possible answers to the greatest possible number of different questions.
It appears instead as the art of asking those questions in the best possible way.
That is the aspect of philosophy to which we must now turn.
2. Philosophy as the ability to ask questions

In one sense, philosophy properly begins at the place and moment when a proposition previously regarded as true is, for the first time, “called into question”—without being judged false because of any internal contradiction or because it conflicts with evidence supplied by experimental verification, whether technical or political.
The same applies when a proposition previously regarded as false is reopened and therefore placed in question, even though no new reason has appeared for considering it true.
In other words, what characterizes philosophy is doubt about the truth or falsity of claims that have been asserted or rejected.

Any proposition therefore becomes philosophical, in a sense, as soon as we stop treating it as a truth or error settled once and for all and begin treating it instead as the subject of an investigation.
In this respect, philosophy is diametrically opposed to mythmaking: to the natural human tendency to regard every claim we make ourselves, or hear from someone else, as either true or false.

Philosophy is precisely the human capacity to refrain from treating any proposition as simply true or false, and instead to investigate it while “suspending judgment”—or, if you prefer, the capacity to “doubt” any assertion whatsoever.
But this philosophy, which stands opposed to mythmaking, must not be confused with sceptical philosophy.
Scepticism denies that human beings can genuinely distinguish truth from falsehood and therefore treats the “suspension of judgment” as the one attitude that must be maintained permanently.
Philosophy, by contrast, regards the suspension of judgment as only a temporary necessity.
Its doubt is not an end in itself. It is simply a means of establishing the truth once and for all.
